title: Classification into Groups, Periods and Blocks
topicTitle: Classification of elements into different groups, periods and blocks
notes: **Groups (vertical columns):** There are 18 groups in the modern periodic table. Elements in a group share the same number of valence electrons and therefore show similar chemical properties. Group 1 (alkali metals): Li, Na, K, Rb, Cs, Fr — all ns$^1$, form +1 ions. Group 17 (halogens): F, Cl, Br, I, At — all ns$^2$np$^5$, form -1 ions and diatomic molecules (F$_2$, Cl$_2$, Br$_2$, I$_2$).

**Periods (horizontal rows):** There are 7 periods. The period number equals the principal quantum number n of the outermost shell. Period 1 has 2 elements (H, He). Periods 2–3 are short periods (8 elements each). Periods 4–5 are long periods (18 elements each). Periods 6–7 are very long periods (32 elements each, including f-block).

**s-block (Groups 1–2):** Valence electrons occupy the ns orbital. General configuration: ns$^{1-2}$. These are all metals (except H). They are highly reactive, especially with water: 2Na(s) + 2H$_2$O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H$_2$(g). Ionization energies are relatively low; they readily lose electrons to form M$^+$ or M$^{2+}$ ions.

**p-block (Groups 13–18):** Valence configuration: ns$^2$np$^{1-6}$. This block contains all non-metals, metalloids, and many metals. Group 13 (boron family): ns$^2$np$^1$ — B (metalloid), Al, Ga, In, Tl (metals). Group 14 (carbon family): ns$^2$np$^2$ — C, Si (metalloid), Ge, Sn, Pb. Group 15 (nitrogen family): ns$^2$np$^3$ — N, P (non-metals), As, Sb (metalloids), Bi (metal). Group 16 (chalcogens): ns$^2$np$^4$ — O, S, Se, Te, Po. Group 17 (halogens): ns$^2$np$^5$. Group 18 (noble gases): ns$^2$np$^6$ (He: 1s$^2$).

**d-block (Groups 3–12):** Transition metals. General valence configuration: (n-1)d$^{1-10}$ns$^{0-2}$. These elements fill the (n-1)d orbitals. They exhibit: (1) variable oxidation states (e.g., Fe$^{2+}$ and Fe$^{3+}$; Mn$^{2+}$, Mn$^{4+}$, Mn$^{7+}$), (2) coloured compounds due to d-d transitions, (3) catalytic properties (Fe for Haber process, Ni for hydrogenation), (4) formation of complex ions ([Fe(CN)$_6$]$^{4-}$, [Cu(NH$_3$)$_4$]$^{2+}$), and (5) high melting points and hardness due to strong metallic bonding involving d-electrons.

**f-block (inner transition metals):** Lanthanides (4f series, Z=57–71) and actinides (5f series, Z=89–103). General configuration: (n-2)f$^{1-14}$(n-1)d$^{0-1}$ns$^2$. Lanthanides are relatively stable and non-radioactive (except Pm). All actinides are radioactive; U and Pu are important nuclear fuels. The 4f and 5f electrons are deeply buried and do not participate significantly in bonding, making the chemistry of f-block elements dominated by the +3 oxidation state.

**Naming conventions for groups:** Group 1: alkali metals (except H). Group 2: alkaline earth metals. Group 17: halogens (meaning 'salt-formers' — e.g., NaCl from Na + Cl$_2$). Group 18: noble gases or inert gases. The d-block groups (3–12) are sometimes referred to by their old naming (e.g., Group 6: chromium family, Group 11: copper family).

**Period 1 — only 2 elements:** Hydrogen (1s$^1$) and helium (1s$^2$). Helium is placed in Group 18 despite having no p-electrons, because its filled 1s$^2$ shell gives it the same chemical inertness as the ns$^2$np$^6$ noble gases. Hydrogen is uniquely placed — it can lose an electron like alkali metals (H$^+$) or gain one like halogens (H$^-$).

**Period 4 — the first long period:** Contains 18 elements from K (Z=19) to Kr (Z=36). It introduces the first d-block series (Sc–Zn) and completes the first p-block row. The 4s orbital fills before 3d (aufbau principle): K [Ar]4s$^1$, Ca [Ar]4s$^2$, then Sc [Ar]3d$^1$4s$^2$ through Zn [Ar]3d$^{10}$4s$^2$, then Ga [Ar]3d$^{10}$4s$^2$4p$^1$ through Kr [Ar]3d$^{10}$4s$^2$4p$^6$.

**Period 6 — the longest naturally occurring period:** Contains 32 elements from Cs (Z=55) to Rn (Z=86). After Ba (6s$^2$), the 4f subshell fills (Ce–Lu, the lanthanides), then the 5d subshell, then 6p. This is why the lanthanides are shown separately — including them in the main table would make it 32 columns wide.

**Metallic character trends:** Metallic character increases down a group (easier to lose electrons as size increases) and decreases across a period (increasing nuclear charge holds electrons more tightly). Thus, francium is the most metallic element; fluorine is the most non-metallic. The 'staircase' line separating metals from non-metals runs along B–Si–Ge–As–Sb–Te–Po.

**Isoelectronic species:** Ions or atoms with the same number of electrons but different nuclear charges. Example: O$^{2-}$, F$^-$, Ne, Na$^+$, Mg$^{2+}$ all have 10 electrons (1s$^2$2s$^2$2p$^6$). Among isoelectronic species, radius decreases as nuclear charge increases: Mg$^{2+}$ < Na$^+$ < Ne < F$^-$ < O$^{2-}$. This is a direct consequence of the effective nuclear charge.

**Lanthanoid contraction:** The steady decrease in atomic and ionic radii across the lanthanide series (La to Lu) due to poor shielding by 4f electrons. This causes the 4d and 5d transition series elements in the same group to have very similar sizes (e.g., Zr and Hf both have radii ~160 pm), making their separation extremely difficult. It also explains why Au (5d) is smaller than Ag (4d) is not the case — they are nearly the same size.

**Periodic classification practical significance:** The table organises ~118 known elements so that trends in reactivity, bonding, and physical properties can be predicted. For example, knowing that a new element is in Period 7, Group 17 (tennessine, Z=117) allows chemists to predict it will be a solid, less reactive than astatine, and likely form -1 ions.

**Block comparison summary:** s-block elements form ionic compounds and have low IE. p-block elements can form ionic (metals) or covalent (non-metals) compounds, with a wide range of oxidation states. d-block elements form coloured coordination complexes and show variable oxidation states. f-block elements are all metallic, mostly +3 ions, and many are radioactive.

**Diagonal relationship:** Certain pairs of elements in diagonally adjacent positions show similar properties due to similar charge-to-size ratios. Examples: Li and Mg (both form nitrides, carbonates decompose on heating), Be and Al (amphoteric oxides), B and Si (both form covalent hydrides and acidic oxides). This arises from the opposing effects of moving right (increasing IE) and moving down (decreasing IE) a group.

Understanding the group/period/block classification gives immediate access to an element's expected chemistry — without needing to memorise individual properties. The position of an element in the periodic table is its chemical identity card.
confusion: Group 18 noble gases vs. Group 2 alkaline earth metals: Both can have ns$^2$ configuration (He is 1s$^2$, Be is 2s$^2$), but He is placed in Group 18 because its filled shell gives chemical inertness, while Be has a filled s-subshell but is a reactive metal with 2s$^2$ as its valence configuration in a larger atom.

Transition metals are NOT just any metal in the middle of the table: IUPAC defines a transition metal as an element whose atom has an incomplete d sub-shell, or which can give rise to cations with an incomplete d sub-shell. Zn, Cd, Hg (Group 12) are often excluded because they have d$^{10}$ configurations and form only M$^{2+}$ ions with filled d shells.

Period number vs. principal quantum number: Period 4 elements have their valence electrons in the n=4 shell, but the d-electrons being filled belong to n=3 (the 3d orbitals). The period number refers to the highest n value, not the sum.

Metalloids are NOT a separate category from metals and non-metals: They are elements (B, Si, Ge, As, Sb, Te, Po) that exhibit intermediate properties — they are semiconductors, form amphoteric oxides, and can behave as either metals or non-metals depending on reaction conditions.

The f-block elements are NOT periods 6 and 7 'missing': They belong to periods 6 and 7 respectively (lanthanides have 4f filling with n=6 as the outermost shell; actinides have 5f filling with n=7 as the outermost shell), but are placed below the main table for compactness.
practice: An element has the electron configuration 1s$^2$2s$^2$2p$^6$3s$^2$3p$^4$. (a) Which group and period does it belong to? (b) What is its valence electron configuration? (c) Predict whether it forms cations or anions, and write the formula of its sodium salt. (d) Is it a metal, non-metal, or metalloid?

Arrange the following isoelectronic species in order of increasing ionic radius: S$^{2-}$, Cl$^-$, K$^+$, Ca$^{2+}$. Explain your reasoning using the concept of effective nuclear charge. All have 18 electrons.
Classify the following elements by block, group, and period: (a) Z=11 (b) Z=26 (c) Z=34 (d) Z=56 (e) Z=79. For each, write the valence electron configuration and predict the most common ion formed.

Explain the diagonal relationship between lithium and magnesium. List three specific chemical similarities between Li and Mg that distinguish them from the rest of their respective groups. (Hint: consider nitride formation, carbonate thermal stability, and solubility of fluorides/carbonates).

The lanthanoid contraction causes zirconium (Zr, 4d series) and hafnium (Hf, 5d series) to have almost identical atomic radii (~160 pm). Explain why this makes their chemical separation extremely difficult, and why this difficulty would not exist between calcium (Ca) and strontium (Sr).
universalFacts: The 18-group numbering system (IUPAC, 1988) replaced the older system of A/B groups and Roman numerals, providing a universal standard. Group numbers 1–2 are s-block; 3–12 are d-block; 13–18 are p-block.

There are exactly 40 naturally occurring elements (Z=1 to Z=92, excluding Tc and Pm which are synthetic). The remaining ~78 elements have been produced artificially in nuclear reactors or particle accelerators.

The heaviest known element is oganesson (Og, Z=118), a synthetic element with a half-life of less than a millisecond. Its position in Group 18, Period 7 makes it the expected analogue of radon, but relativistic effects may make it quite different.
The d-block contains 40 elements across 4 series (3d, 4d, 5d, 6d). The 6d series is incomplete — elements 104–112 belong to it, and elements beyond 112 are expected to continue filling 6d before 7p.

The classification of elements into blocks based on the subshell being filled (s, p, d, f) directly reflects the quantum mechanical structure of the atom and provides a theoretical foundation for the periodic table's organisation.
